draft.title: Sexual reproduction
card: In sexual reproduction, two parents each make gametes. Gametes are sex cells, such as sperm and egg cells.
A sperm and an egg join in fertilisation. This forms a zygote, which has a mix of genes from both parents.
Each offspring gets a different combination of genes. So offspring differ from each other and from their parents, apart from identical twins.
This variation can help a population survive change, such as a new disease or a hotter climate. Some individuals may have features that suit the new conditions.
draft.remember: Two gametes join, so offspring vary, and variation gives a population a better chance when conditions change.

a.q: Why are offspring from sexual reproduction usually different from their parents?
opts: Each offspring gets a new mix of genes from two gametes
Each offspring gets all of its genes from one parent
Offspring copy their genes from the parent that is stronger
Offspring change their genes to suit their surroundings
a.why: Fertilisation joins two gametes, one from each parent, so each zygote has a new mix of genes. Offspring do not choose or alter their genes to suit their surroundings.
a.clue: Think about what fertilisation joins together.

b.q: A fungus kills many plants in a field of wild daisies that reproduce sexually. Why might some daisies still survive?
opts: Variation means some may carry genes that resist the fungus
The fungus cannot harm plants that have two parents
Each daisy changes its genes to resist the fungus
All the daisies are identical so all are protected
b.why: Sexual reproduction produces varied offspring, so some daisies may carry genes that resist the fungus and survive to breed. Having two parents does not give protection by itself, and individuals do not change their genes to suit a threat.
b.clue: Think about whether the daisies are all the same or not.

a.best: Each offspring gets a new mix of genes from two gametes

b.best: Variation means some may carry genes that resist the fungus

problems.detail: "So offspring differ from each other and from their parents, apart from identical twins" can be read as saying identical twins do not differ from their parents. Identical twins share genes with each other, but still have a new mix that differs from each parent. It also clashes with the line before, "Each offspring gets a different combination of genes". Suggest: "So offspring differ from their parents and from each other (except identical twins, who share the same genes as each other)."
